pages.x: From 1929 Joseph Stalin forced the Soviet Union's peasants to give up their own farms and join huge collective farms run by the state. Millions resisted, killing their animals rather than hand them over. Better-off farmers, called kulaks, were shot or sent to Siberia by the hundred thousand.

In 1932 the harvest in Ukraine was poor, but Moscow kept raising the grain it demanded, and brigades searched houses and took everything, even seed. Taking a few ears of grain from a field could mean death or ten years in the camps, and villages that fell short were cut off from all goods.

In the spring of 1933 people in the Ukrainian countryside were dying by the thousand every day. In January Stalin had banned starving peasants from leaving Ukraine to look for food, and all the while the Soviet Union went on selling grain abroad.
pages.of: people died in Ukraine, by most estimates

pages.x: A young Welsh reporter, Gareth Jones, walked through Ukrainian villages in March 1933 and told the world of the famine. Soviet officials denied it, and some Western reporters in Moscow, among them Walter Duranty of the New York Times, backed the denial. Jones was murdered in Inner Mongolia two years later.

Ukraine suffered most, but not alone. In Kazakhstan, where herding families were forced to settle on collective farms, perhaps a million and a half people, more than a third of all Kazakhs, died of hunger, and many more fled into China.

For decades the Soviet Union denied that the famine had happened. Ukrainians call it the Holodomor, death by hunger, and every November they light candles in their windows to remember it. Ukraine and many other countries call it a genocide of the Ukrainian people; some historians see it as a crime against all Soviet peasants.
pts: Caused by the seizure of grain, 1932 and 1933
